title: Filter male employees older than 30 from the "Sales" department.
shortTitle: Filter male employees older than 30 from the "Sales" department

s1_definition.profdef: This is a multi-condition `filter` where the predicate is the logical AND of three separate tests — gender, age, and department — so an element survives only when all three are simultaneously true. Each test is a boolean expression and the stream evaluates them lazily for every element.
s1_definition.analogy: The HR manager at the National Bank of India now has three rules at the door: "You must be male, AND older than 30, AND in the Sales department." Only a person who satisfies every one of the three rules walks through. Fail any single rule and you are stopped.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a multi-condition `filter` where the predicate is the logical AND of three separate tests — gender, age, and department — so an element survives only when all three are simultaneously true. Each test is a boolean expression and the stream evaluates them lazily for every element.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR manager at the National Bank of India now has three rules at the door: "You must be male, AND older than 30, AND in the Sales department." Only a person who satisfies every one of the three rules walks through. Fail any single rule and you are stopped.

**One line to remember:** Chain as many conditions as you need with logical AND so an element passes only when every rule is satisfied.

sections.s2_technical:
When three conditions must all hold, you write one predicate joining them with the AND operator, for example `e -> "M".equals(e.getGender()) && e.getAge() > 30 && "Sales".equals(e.getDepartment())`. The stream calls this predicate once per employee and keeps only the ones where the whole expression is true.

The order of the conditions matters a little for performance because of short-circuiting. Java evaluates left to right and stops at the first false. If most of your data is not in Sales, putting the cheap and highly selective department check first means the age and gender checks are skipped for the majority of records. This is a real optimization in large banking datasets.

For age, "older than 30" means strictly greater than 30, so someone who is exactly 30 does not qualify. For gender and department we compare Strings with the equals method and put the constant on the left, which is a null-safe habit that avoids a `NullPointerException` if the field is null.

A senior nuance: three inline conditions are fine, but if these rules are business policy you often extract them into named `Predicate` constants and combine with `and`, which makes the policy readable and testable in isolation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a senior relationship-manager mentoring programme. The policy committee defined the mentor profile precisely: a male employee, older than 30, working in the Sales department, because these are the experienced field staff who close high-value current accounts like Priya's. HR holds the full staff list and needs to extract exactly this profile. This is exactly how a three-condition filter works — each employee is tested for gender, age, and department, and only those who satisfy all three become mentors.

The code defines an `Employee` with name, gender, age and department. A `MentorService` exposes `selectMentors(List<Employee>)` that filters with the three-way AND predicate. The runnable `Main` feeds a varied list and logs the chosen mentors.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (M, 34, Sales), Arjun (M, 28, Sales), Priya (F, 35, Sales), Mohan (M, 45, IT), Karan (M, 41, Sales).

Step 1: The stream opens over five employees.

Step 2: Rajesh enters. Sales is true, age 34 greater than 30 is true, gender M is true — all three pass, Rajesh is a mentor.

Step 3: Arjun enters. Sales true, but age 28 is not greater than 30, so the AND fails and Arjun is dropped.

Step 4: Priya enters. Sales true, age 35 true, but gender M is false, so Priya is dropped.

Step 5: Mohan enters. Department Sales is false right away, so short-circuit drops Mohan without checking age or gender.

Step 6: Karan enters. Sales true, 41 greater than 30 true, M true — Karan is a mentor.

Step 7: `collect` gathers Rajesh and Karan.

```
  stream()
    │
    ▼
  filter(dept==Sales && age>30 && gender==M)

    ├─ Priya   Sales ✓ 35>30 ✓ M ✗  → DROP │
    ├─ Mohan   IT ✗ (short-circuit)   → DROP │

                                            ▼
  collect(toList())  →  [Rajesh, Karan]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When several conditions must all hold, I build a single predicate that joins them with logical AND, so an element survives the filter only when every one of the tests is true. In this case the mentor profile needed three things at once — the person had to be male, older than thirty, and in the Sales department — so my predicate combined all three with the AND operator and the stream kept only the employees who satisfied all of them.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was the mentor-selection logic for the relationship-manager programme. The policy committee wanted experienced male field staff over thirty in Sales, because they close the high-value current accounts, so I filtered the staff list with that three-way condition. I was careful that "older than 30" means strictly greater than thirty, so an employee who is exactly thirty does not qualify.

A senior point I always mention is that the order of the conditions matters because Java short-circuits the AND left to right. I put the cheapest and most selective check — department equals Sales — first, so for the majority of employees who are not in Sales, the age and gender checks are never evaluated at all. On a large dataset that is a genuine performance win. I also compare Strings with the equals method and keep the constant literal on the left-hand side, which is a null-safe habit that prevents a null pointer exception on missing data, and if these rules ever became formal policy I would extract them into named predicates so they are testable on their own.
